questions.q: const ZONES = ["lagos", "abuja"] as const; is followed by type Zone = ZONES;. What does the compiler say, and why?
questions.explain: Values and types live in separate spaces. typeof in a type position is the bridge from a value's name to its type. (typeof ZONES)[number] then gives "lagos" | "abuja".
options: Nothing; a const can be used as a type
That ZONES refers to a value but is used as a type; a type query, typeof ZONES, is needed to cross from values to types
That ZONES must be declared with type instead of const
That arrays cannot be used in types

questions.q: After let currency = "NGN";, what is typeof currency in a type position?
questions.explain: A type query returns the declared type, and a let initialized with a string widens to string because it may be reassigned. With const it would be the literal "NGN". (The string "string" is what the JavaScript typeof operator returns at runtime.)

questions.q: What is typeof shop for const shop = { city: "Lagos", rating: 4.8 };?
questions.explain: The variable is const, but its properties can still be changed, so they are widened. as const would keep the literals and make the properties readonly.

questions.q: For class Invoice { static prefix = "INV"; … }, which type describes the class itself (the thing you call new on)?
questions.explain: In a type position, the class name means the instance type. typeof Invoice is the constructor type, with its static members such as prefix. InstanceType<typeof Invoice> goes back to Invoice.

questions.q: Why is type Shop = typeof loadShop(); a syntax error, and what do you write instead?
questions.explain: Types describe code; they never evaluate it. Take the function's type with typeof loadShop, then ask for the return type with the ReturnType utility.
options: Because a type query takes a name or property path and never runs code; write ReturnType<typeof loadShop>
Because functions have no type; write typeof loadShop.return
Because of a missing semicolon; write typeof (loadShop());

questions.q: Card has keys kind, last4, amountKobo; Transfer has kind, bankCode, amountKobo. What is keyof (Card | Transfer)?
questions.explain: A value of a union type could be either member, so the only keys you can safely use are the ones both have. The union of values has the intersection of keys.

questions.q: Using the same Card and Transfer, what is keyof (Card & Transfer)?
questions.explain: An intersection has every property of both types, so its keys are all the keys of both. (The intersection itself is impossible to create here, because kind would have to be both "card" and "transfer", but keyof still lists the keys.)

questions.q: What is keyof { [reference: string]: Payment }?
questions.explain: JavaScript converts number keys to strings, so payments[42] works on an object with a string index signature. TypeScript therefore includes number in its keyof.

questions.q: Why does function label<T>(key: keyof T) { return `field ${key}`; } fail to compile?
questions.explain: Keys can be strings, numbers or symbols. keyof T & string keeps only the string keys; String(key) converts explicitly when symbols can really occur.
options: Because generic functions cannot use template literals
Because keyof T may include symbol, and converting a symbol to a string in a template throws at runtime
Because keyof T is always never for an unconstrained T

questions.q: With interface Order { id: string; total: number; status: "pending" | "paid" }, what is Order["total" | "status"]?
questions.explain: Indexing with a union of keys gives the union of the property types. To get an object with just those properties, you would use Pick<Order, "total" | "status">.

questions.q: What does Order["lines"][number] mean when lines is an array of line objects?
questions.explain: [number] asks "what do I get when I index this array with any number?": the element type. It is how you name OrderLine without writing its shape again.
options: The type of one element of the lines array
A tuple of all the lines

questions.q: For type Row = [date: string, description: string, amountKobo: number], what are Row["length"] and Row[number]?
questions.explain: A tuple's length is a literal type, because its size is fixed. [number] is any position, so it is the union of all element types.

questions.q: interface Order { couponCode?: string }. What is Order["couponCode"]?
questions.explain: An optional property may be missing, and reading a missing property gives undefined, so the looked-up type includes it.

questions.q: Why does const STATUSES = ["pending", "paid"]; type Status = (typeof STATUSES)[number]; give string instead of "pending" | "paid"?
questions.explain: A mutable array widens its elements. as const makes it readonly ["pending", "paid"], and then [number] gives the union of the two literals.
options: Because without as const the array is inferred as string[], so its elements are string
Because arrays cannot be used with typeof

questions.q: Why check a lookup table with as const satisfies Record<string, number> rather than annotating it : Record<string, number>?
questions.explain: A variable's type is what you declare. satisfies checks the value against a type without changing the value's inferred type, which is what you derive from. Neither checks anything at runtime.
options: Because annotations are slower to compile
Because the annotation replaces the table's own type, so keyof typeof becomes string; satisfies checks the shape and keeps the literal keys and values
Because satisfies also validates the data at runtime
Because an annotation makes the object mutable

questions.q: Why does Object.keys(stock) return string[] even when stock: Stock has only the keys rice and beans?
questions.explain: Structural typing lets { rice: 12, beans: 5, lastCountedBy: "Tunde" } be passed as a Stock. Object.keys would then also return "lastCountedBy". Loop over a known key list instead.
options: Because TypeScript forgot to type it
Because a value may have more properties than its type lists; typing the result as (keyof Stock)[] would be a lie for such values
Because keys are always strings at runtime and TypeScript cannot track literal strings

questions.q: Why is product[key] = value rejected with "not assignable to type never" when key: keyof Product and value: Product[keyof Product]?
questions.explain: Otherwise updateField(product, "priceKobo", "free") would pass. Reading through a union key gives a union; writing requires the intersection.
options: Because objects cannot be modified in TypeScript
Because the key and value are not connected: writing through a union of keys needs a value that fits every property at once, and string & number & boolean is never
Because keyof cannot be used on interfaces
Because the product must be declared readonly

questions.q: Which signature lets product[key] = value compile while still rejecting updateField(p, "priceKobo", "free")?
questions.explain: A type parameter ties the value's type to the chosen key: each call picks one K, and the value must be Product[K]. The any version compiles but accepts nonsense.
options: (product: Product, key: keyof Product, value: any)
<K extends keyof Product>(product: Product, key: K, value: Product[K])
(product: Product, key: keyof Product, value: Product)

questions.q: NEXT[from] has type readonly ["paid", "cancelled"] | readonly []. Why is NEXT[from].includes(to) an error?
questions.explain: Assign to a wider type first, which is safe without an assertion: const next: readonly Status[] = NEXT[from];, then next.includes(to).
options: Because includes does not exist on readonly arrays
Because calling a method on a union needs an argument that suits every member, and the empty tuple's includes accepts only never

questions.q: Why does isOrderStatus use Object.hasOwn(ORDER_FLOW, value) rather than value in ORDER_FLOW?
questions.explain: An object literal inherits from Object.prototype. A status coming from JSON could be "toString" or "constructor"; only own properties are real statuses.
options: Because in does not work on objects created with as const
Because in also finds inherited properties, so "toString" in ORDER_FLOW is true
Because in is not a type guard

questions.q: When is a plain written-out union like type Role = "customer" | "staff" a better choice than deriving it from an as const array?
questions.explain: Derive from a value when the program needs that value (a dropdown, validation, iteration). Otherwise the array is extra code, and the union alone is the simplest single source of truth.
options: When nothing at runtime needs the list of roles
When there are more than ten roles
When the roles are used in a switch

questions.q: Here typeof appears in both roles. What does this print?
questions.explain: In an expression, typeof is JavaScript's runtime operator and returns a string such as "object". The type query in type Shop = typeof shop is erased and prints nothing.
options: { name: string; rating: number } number string

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: shelf is a variable, not a fresh object literal, so its extra garri property is allowed. Object.keys returns all three keys, and the as keyof Stock hid that from the compiler.
options: It does not compile: shelf has an extra property

questions.q: keyof { 0: string; 1: string } is 0 | 1. What does this print at runtime?
questions.explain: Property keys are strings (or symbols) at runtime; JavaScript converts number keys to strings. TypeScript's numeric literal keys describe how you may index the object, not what Object.keys returns.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same SIZES array is the runtime list and the source of the Size type. filter is available on readonly arrays (it returns a new array); only mutating methods such as push are removed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: in walks the prototype chain, so the inherited toString is found. Object.hasOwn only checks the object's own properties, which is what a lookup table needs.
options:
abuja true true
toString true false
kano false false

abuja true true
toString false false
kano false false

abuja true true
toString true true
kano false false

abuja true false

questions.q: as const makes this array readonly in the type system. What does it print at runtime?
questions.explain: as const is a compile-time instruction and is erased; the array is an ordinary array at runtime. Object.freeze is the runtime equivalent, and TypeScript types its result as readonly too.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The function returns a new object with the spread, so mug is unchanged. The computed key [key] overwrites only priceKobo.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each lookup reads the table: pending may go to paid, not straight to shipped, and shipped has no next status at all. The widening assignment is what lets includes accept any Status.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Seats is 1 | 5, derived by indexing every plan and then its seats property; it only exists at compile time. At runtime there are two plans, and the team plan costs ₦4,000 (400,000 kobo) per seat.

questions.q: Derive PaymentStatus from the PAYMENT_STATUSES array, and write the type guard isPaymentStatus(value: string): value is PaymentStatus using the same array.
questions.explain: The list is written once and serves both the type and the runtime check. some with === compares a string against each literal without the includes parameter problem of a readonly tuple.
questions.expected:
captured true
refunded false
failed true

questions.q: Derive Zone from the keys of DELIVERY_FEES, write fee(zone: Zone): number, and print the fee for each zone in ZONES_TO_QUOTE in naira.
questions.explain: keyof typeof DELIVERY_FEES is "lagos" | "abuja" | "kano", so DELIVERY_FEES[zone] needs no cast, and a typo in ZONES_TO_QUOTE would not compile. satisfies checked the fees are numbers without widening the keys.

questions.q: Write getField<T, K extends keyof T>(item: T, key: K): T[K], then use it to print a booking's seat in upper case and its nights doubled.
questions.explain: Each call picks its own K, so seat is a string and nights a number: no conversions needed. The any version needed String and Number because it knew nothing.

questions.q: Finish setField so it changes one property of a room in place, keeping the key and value connected with a type parameter.
questions.explain: With K as a type parameter, value is exactly the type of the chosen property, and the write room[key] = value is allowed. With a plain union key, the write needs never.

questions.q: Finish canMove using the NEXT table. NEXT[from].includes(to) does not compile on the union of tuples, so assign NEXT[from] to a wider type first (no as).
questions.explain: Every tuple in the table is assignable to readonly BookingStatus[], so the assignment is safe, and on the wider array includes accepts any status.

questions.q: totalBags adds up the wrong things when an object carries extra properties. Rewrite it to loop over the known ITEMS list instead of Object.keys.
questions.explain: The known list only contains keys the type promises, so no assertion is needed and extra runtime properties such as crates are ignored. The starter's as keyof Stock let crates slip into the sum.

questions.q: Name the type of one cart line with an indexed access type on Cart (do not write its shape again), and write lineTotal(line: CartLine): number. Print the cart total.
questions.explain: Cart["lines"] is the array type and [number] its element type. If a field is later added to cart lines, CartLine follows automatically.

questions.q: Write describeFields<T extends object>(item: T, keys: readonly (keyof T & string)[]): string that returns "key=value" pairs joined with ", ". The & string is what allows the template literal.
questions.explain: keyof T & string drops number and symbol keys, so `${key}` is safe. The value is converted with String because T[K] could be anything, including a symbol.
